title: Problems: dead zones, barriers, meta-labels and overlap

items.prose: An index fund closes at £64.00 on day 0, and its recent daily volatility is $\sigma = 1.6\%$. A desk labels day 0 two ways over $h = 4$ days. One is a dead-zone label with $k = 0.75$. The other is a triple barrier at $\pm 2\sigma$ with a 4-day limit. The next four closes are £63.10, £62.40, £61.90 and £65.28.

parts.question: What is the dead-zone bar $k\sigma\sqrt{h}$? Give a percentage to 1 decimal place.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Multiply $k$, $\sigma$ and $\sqrt{h}$.

byKey.no-root: That is $k\sigma$, a one-day bar. A 4-day return spreads $\sqrt{4} = 2$ times wider.
byKey.times-h: You scaled by $h = 4$. The spread grows with $\sqrt{h} = 2$, not with $h$.

explain.text: A 4-day return has spread about $\sigma\sqrt{4} = 3.2\%$. The bar is $k = 0.75$ of that: $2.4\%$.

parts.question: Using the bar of 2.4% from part 1, what dead-zone label does day 0 get? Type $-1$, $0$ or $1$.

feedback.correct: Day 4 closes at £65.28, a return of $65.28/64 - 1 = 2.0\%$, inside the 2.4% bar: label 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare the 4-day return with the 2.4% bar.

byKey.sign-only: The close rose, but by 2.0%, inside the 2.4% bar. A narrower bar, such as the one-day 1.2%, would give $+1$.

explain.text: The fixed-horizon label reads only day 0 and day 4: $65.28/64.00 - 1 = 0.020$. That is inside $\pm 2.4\%$, so the label is 0.

parts.question: Where is the lower barrier of the triple barrier, in pounds to the nearest penny?

feedback.generic: Not quite. The lower barrier is $P_0(1 - k\sigma)$ with $k = 2$.

byKey.root-h: You widened the barrier by $\sqrt{h}$. Barriers sit at $\pm k\sigma$ from the entry, using the daily $\sigma$.
byKey.one-sigma: That is one $\sigma$ below. The barrier is at $2\sigma$: $64.00 \times 0.968$.

explain.text: The barriers are set at entry from that day's volatility. With $k = 2$ and $\sigma = 1.6\%$ they sit 3.2% away: £66.05 above and £61.95 below.

parts.question: Using the lower barrier of £61.95 from part 3, what does `first_touch` return for day 0?

options.why: Day 2 closes at £62.40, still above the £61.95 barrier.
Day 3's close of £61.90 is below £61.95, so the trade ends before the limit.
Day 4's £65.28 is below the upper barrier of £66.05, and the trade has already ended.

feedback.correct: Day 3 closes at £61.90, at or below £61.95: the stop ends the trade after 3 days.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Walk the closes in order and stop at the first one outside £61.95 to £66.05.

byKey.stop-2: Day 2 closes at £62.40, still above the £61.95 barrier.
byKey.time: Day 3's close of £61.90 is below £61.95, so the trade ends before the limit.
byKey.profit: Day 4's £65.28 is below the upper barrier of £66.05, and the trade has already ended.

explain.text: £63.10 and £62.40 stay inside the band, and £61.90 breaks the stop on day 3. The first touch wins, so day 4's recovery is never read.

parts.question: Using the exit from part 4, what return did the trade make? Give a percentage to 2 decimal places.

feedback.correct: The trade sells at day 3's close: $61.90/64.00 - 1 = -3.28\%$, while the dead zone said 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite. The trade sells at the close that broke the stop, £61.90.

byKey.at-barrier: That is the barrier, £61.95 or 3.2% down. With closes only, the sale is at the close that crossed it, £61.90.
byKey.day-four: That is the day 4 return the fixed-horizon label used. The trade was stopped out on day 3.
byKey.no-sign: The size is right, but the price fell from £64.00 to £61.90: the return is negative.

explain.text: The close-only rule sells at £61.90, a loss of 3.28%. The fixed-horizon label calls day 0 a non-event, though the managed trade lost money.

items.prose:
A breakout rule on a copper miner picks a side for twelve trades. Each trade runs under triple barriers, labelled $+1$ upper, $-1$ lower, $0$ time. A secondary model gives each trade a probability $p$ that the call pays.

| trade | side | barrier label | $p$ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | $+1$ | $+1$ | 0.74 |
| 2 | $-1$ | $-1$ | 0.61 |
| 3 | $+1$ | $-1$ | 0.58 |
| 4 | $+1$ | $0$ | 0.33 |
| 5 | $-1$ | $+1$ | 0.47 |
| 6 | $+1$ | $+1$ | 0.69 |
| 7 | $-1$ | $-1$ | 0.52 |
| 8 | $+1$ | $-1$ | 0.63 |
| 9 | $-1$ | $0$ | 0.29 |
| 10 | $+1$ | $+1$ | 0.81 |
| 11 | $-1$ | $0$ | 0.41 |
| 12 | $+1$ | $-1$ | 0.66 |

parts.question: How many of the twelve meta-labels are 1?

feedback.correct: Trades 1, 2, 6, 7 and 10 have side times label equal to 1: five calls paid.
feedback.generic: Not quite. A meta-label is 1 when side times label is 1.

byKey.price-up: You counted the labels of $+1$, the price rising. A short pays on $-1$: trades 2 and 7 paid.
byKey.time-wins: You counted the three time-outs as wins. A trade that times out did not take its profit, so its meta-label is 0.

explain.text: The products $s_i y_i$ are $1, 1, -1, 0, -1, 1, 1, -1, 0, 1, 0, -1$. Five equal 1, so 5 meta-labels are 1: two shorts that fell and three longs that rose.

parts.question: Using the 5 paying calls from part 1, what is the base rate, the precision at threshold 0? Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.correct: Threshold 0 takes all twelve trades, and 5 pay: $5/12 = 0.4167$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. At threshold 0 every trade is taken, so precision is the share that paid.

byKey.price-up: That is $4/12$, from counting price rises. Five calls paid.
byKey.time-wins: That is $8/12$, counting time-outs as wins. Five calls paid.

explain.text: Acting on every call is the breakout rule alone. Its hit rate, $5/12 = 0.4167$, is the bar the filter must clear.

parts.question: The desk acts when $p \ge 0.6$. What is the precision? Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.correct: Trades 1, 2, 6, 8, 10 and 12 are taken, and 1, 2, 6 and 10 pay: $4/6 = 0.6667$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Precision divides the taken trades that paid by the trades taken.

byKey.recall: That is $4/5$, the share of paying calls kept: recall. Precision divides by the 6 trades taken.
byKey.share-taken: That is $6/12$, the share of trades taken. Of those 6, four paid.

explain.text: Six trades have $p \ge 0.6$, and four of them have meta-label 1. Precision is $4/6 = 0.6667$, against the base rate of 0.4167.

parts.question: Using the 5 paying calls from part 1, what is the recall at $p \ge 0.6$? Give a decimal.

feedback.correct: Four of the 5 paying calls are taken: $4/5 = 0.8$. Trade 7, with $p = 0.52$, is the one missed.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Recall divides the paying calls taken by all the paying calls.

byKey.precision: That is $4/6$, the precision. Recall divides by the 5 calls that paid.
byKey.price-up: That is $3/4$, from part 1's price-rise count. The paying calls are 1, 2, 6, 7 and 10.

explain.text: The filter keeps trades 1, 2, 6 and 10 of the five winners and drops trade 7. Recall is $4/5 = 0.8$.

parts.question: Using precision 0.6667 and recall 0.8, what is the F1 score? Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. F1 is $\frac{2PR}{P + R}$.

byKey.mean: That is the plain average of the two. F1 is the harmonic mean, $\frac{2PR}{P + R}$.
byKey.product: That is $P \times R$. Double it and divide by $P + R$.

explain.text: With $P = \tfrac23$ and $R = \tfrac45$, F1 is $\tfrac{16/15}{22/15} = \tfrac{8}{11} = 0.7273$. The filter lifts precision from 0.4167 to 0.6667 and keeps four winners in five.

items.prose:
Five trades on a silver fund are labelled by `first_touch`, which returns each trade's days held. Each window covers the entry day through the exit day, both ends included. The meta-label says whether the call paid.

| trade | entry day | days held | meta-label |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| A | 0 | 2 | 1 |
| B | 1 | 4 | 0 |
| C | 2 | 2 | 1 |
| D | 4 | 3 | 1 |
| E | 6 | 2 | 0 |

parts.question: How many windows cover day 4? That count is the concurrency $c_4$.

feedback.correct: B covers days 1 to 5, C days 2 to 4 and D days 4 to 7: $c_4 = 3$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Turn each entry and days held into a window, exit day included.

byKey.exit-left-out: You left out C, whose exit day is day 4. The exit day's close decides the label, so it belongs to the window.

explain.text: A runs from day 0 to 2 and B from 1 to 5. C runs 2 to 4, D 4 to 7 and E 6 to 8. Day 4 sits in B, C and D, so $c_4 = 3$.

parts.question: What is label A's average uniqueness? Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Average $1/c_t$ over days 0, 1 and 2.

byKey.invert-mean: You averaged $c_t$ to 2, then inverted it. Average the shares $1/c_t$ instead.
byKey.sum: That is the sum of $1/c_t$. Divide by A's 3 days.

explain.text: Day 0 is A's alone, day 1 is shared with B, and day 2 with B and C. A owns $1 + \tfrac12 + \tfrac13 = \tfrac{11}{6}$ of its 3 days: $\tfrac{11}{18} = 0.6111$.

parts.question: The other weights are B 0.4333, C 0.3889, D 0.4583 and E 0.6667. Using A's 0.6111 from part 2, what is the effective number of labels? Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. The effective number is the sum of the five weights.

byKey.count: That counts each label as a whole one. Overlap makes them worth only their weights: add those.

explain.text: Five overlapping labels carry $\tfrac{307}{120} = 2.5583$ labels' worth of evidence. That sum is the $n$ a standard error should use.

parts.question: Using $n_{\text{eff}} = 2.5583$ from part 3, what is the uniqueness-weighted hit rate of the meta-labels? Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Add the weights of the labels with meta-label 1 and divide by 2.5583.

byKey.unweighted: That is $3/5$, each label counted once. Weight each label by its uniqueness.

explain.text: The winners hold $1.4583$ of the $2.5583$ weight, so the weighted hit rate is $\tfrac{175}{307} = 0.5700$. The heavily shared label C counts for less than A.

parts.question: Using the weighted hit rate 0.5700 and $n_{\text{eff}} = 2.5583$, what is the honest standard error of the hit rate? Give 3 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Put $p = 0.5700$ and $n = 2.5583$ into $\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$.

byKey.naive-n: You used $n = 5$. Overlap leaves only 2.5583 labels' worth of evidence.
byKey.unweighted: You used the unweighted 0.6 with $n_{\text{eff}}$. Use the weighted 0.5700 from part 4.

explain.text: The error is $\sqrt{0.2451/2.5583} = 0.310$, against 0.221 with the naive $n = 5$. Overlap widens the uncertainty by $\sqrt{5/2.5583} = 1.4$ times.

items.prose: A sign model for a bond future is tested on 400 consecutive daily rows. Row $t$'s fixed-horizon label covers days $t + 1$ to $t + 10$. In the test block 57% of the labels are $+1$, and the model's calls are right on 60.5% of rows.

parts.question: Away from the ends of the block, every day is covered by 10 labels. What is the average uniqueness of a label there? Give a decimal.

feedback.correct: Each of its 10 days has $c_t = 10$, so $\bar u = \tfrac{1}{10} = 0.1$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Average $1/c_t$ over the label's days, with $c_t = 10$ on each.

byKey.shared-share: That is the share of days a label shares with its neighbour, 9 of 10. Uniqueness averages $1/c_t$.

explain.text: Ten labels sit on every middle day, so each owns a tenth of it. A middle label has $\bar u = 0.1$: a tenth of an independent one.

parts.question: How many distinct days do the 400 windows cover together?

feedback.correct: Number the rows 1 to 400. The windows then run from day 2 to day 410: 409 days.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Count from the first window's first day to the last window's last day.

byKey.rows: The last row's window runs 10 days past it, so the windows reach 9 days beyond the 400 rows.
byKey.plus-ten: The windows start one day after their rows, so the span is $400 + 10 - 1 = 409$ days.

explain.text: With rows $1$ to $400$, the windows run from day 2 to day 410: $410 - 2 + 1 = 409$ days. Consecutive windows of length 10 add one new day each after the first.

parts.question: Each covered day gives its labels shares $1/c_t$ that add to 1. Each label then divides by its 10 days. Using the 409 days from part 2, what is $n_{\text{eff}}$? Give a decimal to 1 place.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Summing $\bar u_i$ over labels gives the covered days divided by 10.

byKey.middle-only: That is $400 \times 0.1$, as if every label were a middle one. The labels near the ends own more: $409/10$.
byKey.no-divide: That is the covered days. Each label's weight divides its days' shares by its 10 days.

explain.text: $\sum_i \bar u_i = \tfrac{1}{10}\sum_i \sum_{t \in i} \tfrac{1}{c_t} = \tfrac{1}{10} \times 409$, because each covered day's shares add to 1. So 400 rows carry 40.9 labels' worth of evidence.

parts.question: Using $n_{\text{eff}} = 40.9$ from part 3, what is the standard error of the hit rate, taking $p = 0.605$? Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Put $p = 0.605$ and $n = 40.9$ into $\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$.

byKey.naive-n: You used $n = 400$. The overlapping rows carry only 40.9 labels' worth.
byKey.base-p: You used the base rate 0.57. The question asks for $p = 0.605$, the model's hit rate.

explain.text: $0.605 \times 0.395 = 0.239$, and $\sqrt{0.239/40.9} = 0.0764$. That is $\sqrt{400/40.9} \approx 3.1$ times the naive error.

parts.question: Using the error 0.0764 from part 4, what is the $t$ statistic of the model's edge over always saying $+1$? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.correct: Always $+1$ scores 0.57, so the edge is 0.035 and $t = 0.035/0.0764 = 0.46$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. The baseline is the share of $+1$ labels, 0.57. Divide the edge over it by 0.0764.

byKey.coin: You measured the edge over a coin's 0.5. The free baseline here is always $+1$, which scores 0.57.
byKey.naive-n: You divided by the naive error 0.0244, from $n = 400$. Use 0.0764.

explain.text: The model beats the majority guess by 3.5 points, and $0.035/0.0764 = 0.46$ errors is well inside luck. Against a coin with the naive $n$ it would have looked like 4.3 errors.
